faq.a: CT defines the exact location, size, and active bleeding, guiding surgery or interventional radiology.
faq.q: Why is CT preferred if ultrasound is positive?

faq.a: Yes, if the patient is hemodynamically stable, the bleed is contained, and there is no organ injury.
faq.q: Can a retroperitoneal hematoma resolve without surgery?

faq.a: It indicates retroperitoneal hemorrhage; bruising of the flank appears 12‑24 h after bleeding.
faq.q: What is the significance of Grey‑Turner sign?

exam: A 28‑year‑old motorcyclist presents with flank pain, tachycardia and BP 85/50 mmHg. What is your immediate management? — Rapid fluid resuscitation, give tranexamic acid, obtain FAST, prepare for urgent laparotomy if active bleed.
How does a retroperitoneal sarcoma differ from an intra‑abdominal sarcoma on imaging? — It displaces the kidney and vessels, often encases them without breaching the peritoneum.

A patient with known TB develops a left‑flank mass and low‑grade fever. Which test confirms the diagnosis and why? — GeneXpert on aspirated fluid; it rapidly detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and resistance.
What clinical sign helps differentiate a psoas abscess from a retroperitoneal hematoma? — Positive psoas sign (pain on hip flexion) is typical of psoas abscess; hematoma lacks this reproducible pain.
Why is tranexamic acid contraindicated in patients with active thromboembolic disease? — It inhibits fibrinolysis and may worsen existing clots.
When is percutaneous drainage preferred over open surgery for a retroperitoneal collection? — When the collection is well‑encapsulated, patient is stable, and imaging shows a safe access route.

Explain why serum creatinine may be misleading in early retroperitoneal injury. — Creatinine rises only after significant loss of GFR; early injury may present with normal values, so urine output is essential.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt you to call for senior surgical review in a stable patient with a small retroperitoneal hematoma? — Sudden drop in urine output or new onset of anuria.
ai.title: Retroperitoneal Space and Pathology
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: The retroperitoneum is the posterior abdominal compartment that houses kidneys, pancreas, major vessels and lymphatics. Understanding its anatomy, common causes of disease, and how to investigate and manage emergencies is essential for low‑resource settings.

b: Key landmarks: psoas muscle, quadratus lumborum, aorta, IVC, kidneys, pancreas, duodenum (2nd‑4th parts).
Diagnosis is clinical suspicion plus imaging (ultrasound, CT if available).
sections.p: A potential space behind the peritoneum extending from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor. It is divided into anterior (pararenal), perirenal and posterior (posterior pararenal) compartments.

b: Mild: confined fluid, stable vitals.
Moderate: large hematoma or urinoma, mild renal impairment.
Severe: massive hemorrhage, shock, multi‑organ failure.
sections.p: No universal staging; severity is judged by extent of fluid/hematoma, organ injury, and physiologic impact (hemodynamic instability, renal failure).

b: Blunt abdominal or pelvic trauma (road‑traffic collisions, falls).
Penetrating injuries (stab, gunshot).
Infectious: tuberculous lymphadenitis, pyogenic abscess, schistosomal fibrosis.
Neoplastic: retroperitoneal sarcoma (leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma).
Iatrogenic: renal biopsy, ureteric stent placement.
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals trauma and infection dominate.

b: Flank/loin pain radiating to groin.
Tenderness deep to the abdominal wall, not peritoneal rebound.
Visible bruising (Grey‑Turner sign) in severe hemorrhage.
Hematuria if renal injury, oliguria if renal perfusion compromised.
sections.p: Patients often have vague back or flank pain, abdominal distension, and signs of hypovolemia if bleeding.

t.b: Detects free fluid in Morison’s pouch or retroperitoneal collection; positive → consider hemorrhage.
Shows displaced bowel loops, loss of psoas shadow; helps when CT unavailable.
Gold standard for location, size, organ injury, active contrast extravasation.
Assess renal function; rising creatinine suggests renal ischemia or obstruction.

t.a: TB PCR or GeneXpert on aspirate (if infection suspected)
t.b: Confirms tuberculous retroperitoneal abscess; guides anti‑TB therapy.

b: Hemodynamic shock (BP <90 mmHg, tachycardia).
Acute kidney injury (creatinine rise >50%).
Compartment syndrome of the retroperitoneum (pain out of proportion, tense abdomen).
Sepsis from infected collection.
sections.p: Complications arise from ongoing bleeding, infection, or compression of vital structures.

b: IV crystalloid bolus 1‑2 L, then blood transfusion if shock persists.
Urgent surgical exploration for expanding hematoma, active contrast leak, or uncontrolled shock.
Percutaneous drainage of abscesses; give broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) pending culture.
Anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for confirmed tuberculous collections.
Avoid NSAIDs in renal injury; avoid nephrotoxic contrast if renal function already impaired.
sections.p: Initial resuscitation, control of bleeding, and treatment of the underlying cause.

b: Serial creatinine and urine output for 48‑72 h.
Repeat ultrasound at 1‑2 weeks for residual collection.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and tetanus in trauma patients.
Educate on safe road‑use and use of protective gear.
sections.p: Monitor renal function, wound healing, and screen for late complications.

b: Intra‑abdominal (intraperitoneal) hemorrhage – usually presents with peritoneal signs.
Psoas abscess – localized pain, fever, positive psoas sign, often from TB.
Pancreatic pseudocyst – located in lesser sac, not true retroperitoneum.
FAST may miss small retroperitoneal collections; a negative scan does not rule out injury.
Serum lactate can be normal early in hemorrhage; repeat if clinical picture worsens.
Creatinine may be falsely low in low‑muscle patients; use urine output as adjunct.
